extracted.intended_audience: IP attorneys, patent litigators, in-house counsel, and technology companies concerned with U.S. software patents
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation guidance for whether software-implemented inventions satisfy 35 U.S.C. §101 following the Supreme Court's Alice v. CLS Bank decision, focusing on the Mayo/Alice two-step framework and related precedent (Diehr, Benson, Flook, Bilski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101
rubrics_metrics.description: The Patent Act grants patents for any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or improvements thereof (35 U.S.C. §101), but there are implicit exceptions for laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restriction exists to avoid monopolization of basic tools of scientific and technological work that might impede innovation (citing Diamond v. Diehr and Mayo).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-step framework — Step 1: directed to patent-ineligible concept
rubrics_metrics.description: First determine whether the claims are directed to a patent-ineligible concept (e.g., a law of nature, natural phenomenon, or abstract idea).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts must 'identif[y] the abstract idea represented in the claim' and decide if the claim at its core embraces an ineligible building block (as applied in Alice and prior cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-step framework — Step 2: inventive concept / 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claims are directed to an ineligible concept, analyze claim elements individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether they add an 'inventive concept' sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the additions are 'sufficient to ensure that the patent in practice amounts to significantly more than a patent upon the [ineligible concept] itself' (Mayo language).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation does not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere introduction or recitation of a computer into the claims, when that implementation is purely conventional or generic, does not alter the Alice/Mayo analysis or render an abstract idea patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court warned that 'wholly generic computer implementation is not generally the sort of "additional feature" that provides any "practical assurance"' the claim is more than drafting to monopolize the abstract idea. Electronic recordkeeping and other basic computer functions typically will not suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limiting an abstract idea to a particular technological environment is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Restricting performance of an abstract idea to a particular technological environment (e.g., 'implemented via computers') does not by itself make the claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court emphasized that tying an abstract idea to a technological environment is not the same as supplying the inventive concept required under step two (citing Alice and Bilski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diehr exception — improvement to technological process can be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that employ a mathematical formula or abstract concept as part of a computer-implemented process may be eligible where the additional claim steps transform the process into an inventive application by solving a technological problem or improving conventional industry practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diehr is distinguished from Benson/Flook/Alice: in Diehr a thermocouple measurement plus computer recalculation produced a technological improvement not previously obtainable, and that enabled eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to fundamental economic practices are abstract ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to fundamental economic practices long prevalent in commerce (e.g., intermediated settlement) are treated as abstract ideas and thus fall within the Section 101 exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice held that intermediated settlement was a 'building block' of the modern economy and therefore an abstract idea beyond Section 101's scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hardware recitations must provide meaningful limitations beyond generic functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting 'specific hardware' or functional components (e.g., data processing system, communications controller, data storage unit) is not enough if those elements are purely functional and generic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: System and Beauregard (computer-readable medium) claims that merely tie a method to conventional hardware 'offer[] a meaningful limitation beyond generally linking the use of the [method] to a particular technological environment' only if the hardware contributes more than generic implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electronic recordkeeping/basic computer functions are not inventive
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim steps that effectively recite 'electronic recordkeeping' or other of the most basic functions of a computer generally will not transform an abstract idea into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alice described electronic recordkeeping as one of the most basic computer functions and treated such recitations as insufficient under step two.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fact-intensive inquiry: must show more than a known manual procedure on a computer
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility analysis will be fact-intensive and focus on whether a software-based implementation is more than merely performing a known, manual procedure using a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentees must persuade a court or jury that the implementation amounts to significantly more than applying a known human activity via generic computer functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof that invention is a tangible, hardware-based implementation (not just data)
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts may require evidence that the claimed invention is directed to a tangible, hardware-based implementation rather than merely the underlying data or abstract manipulation of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing concrete hardware effects or an improvement in computer functionality helps distinguish eligible inventions from claims to data or abstract ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate improvement on known procedures or previously unattainable solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: An inquiry will consider whether the method or system improves upon a known procedure by providing a solution to a problem that had not previously been achieved (or could not be achieved) without the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Showing a specific technological improvement or new capability can support finding an 'inventive concept' under step two and distinguish the claim from mere automation of prior practices.
